Hungerbitten
HUNG-ger-bit-n
adj. (bitten or wasted by hunger; famished)
From hunger and bitten, the past participle of bite — hunger pictured as a thing with teeth. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Bildad's speech against Job, describing the end of the wicked man.

Biblical Definition

His strength shall be hungerbitten, and destruction shall be ready at his side. Bildad is describing the fate of the wicked, and the phrase is vivid and cruel: not that the man is hungry, but that his strength itself is bitten, gnawed away from within, while ruin waits at his elbow. The next verse presses it further — it shall devour the strength of his skin, even the firstborn of death shall devour his strength. As a general description of what sin does to a man, Bildad is not wrong; Scripture says elsewhere that the young lions do lack, and suffer hunger, but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing. What Bildad is wrong about is the application. He is using true doctrine as a diagnosis of a specific righteous man in the ash heap in front of him, and God says at the end of the book that Bildad and his friends have not spoken of him the thing that is right, as Job hath. The word therefore serves the dictionary twice: as an unforgettable picture of the wasting that follows wickedness, and as a warning about the pastoral use of true sentences.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): pinched or wasted by hunger; starved; used once in Scripture of the wicked man's strength in Bildad's speech.

expand to see more

HUNGERBITTEN, a. Pinched or weakened by hunger.

HUNGER, n. An uneasy sensation occasioned by the want of food; a craving of food.

FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient to sustain the people of a country.

DESTRUCTION, n. Demolition; a pulling down; ruin; the state of being destroyed.

AFFLICTION, n. The state of being afflicted; a state of pain, distress or grief.

Key Scripture

Job 18:12 — "His strength shall be hungerbitten, and destruction shall be ready at his side."

Job 18:13 — "It shall devour the strength of his skin: even the firstborn of death shall devour his strength."

Psa 34:10 — "The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing."

Mat 5:6 — "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled."

Modern Corruption

Suffering is read backwards as proof of secret sin, the friends' method in the book of Job; Scripture keeps the general truth that wickedness wastes a man and denies that affliction is a reliable verdict on any particular sufferer.

expand to see more

Bildad's speech is orthodox and misapplied, which makes it more dangerous than heresy. Every clause of it could be defended from Proverbs. The wicked really are brought down, their light really is put out, their strength really is bitten by hunger in the end. The failure is in the inference: this man is suffering, therefore this man is wicked. God's own verdict closes the book against the three friends and for Job, and the Lord himself refused the same inference when asked who sinned, the blind man or his parents, answering that neither had, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.

The error is alive in two modern dresses. One is the prosperity teaching, which reads health and money as evidence of favour and therefore must read illness and poverty as evidence of the reverse. The other is a therapeutic version that treats every hardship as a symptom to be traced to a cause in the sufferer. The Reformed answer is providence: afflictions are real, purposeful, and fatherly toward the elect, and their meaning is not readable off their surface. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled — a hunger with a promise attached, which Bildad had no category for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ra'eb (H7457), hungry or famished; 'own (H202), strength or vigour; 'eyd (H343), calamity or destruction.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra'eb (H7457) — hungry, famished; with 'own, his strength shall be hungerbitten.

Hebrew 'own (H202) — vigour, wealth, generative strength; what hunger bites.

Hebrew 'eyd (H343) — calamity, destruction; ready at his side.

Hebrew bekowr maveth (H1060, H4194) — the firstborn of death; Bildad's name for the worst disease.

Hebrew chacer (H2637) — to lack, to want; they that seek the LORD shall not want.

Usage

"“His strength shall be hungerbitten” — the single occurrence, in Bildad's second speech."

"“The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger” — the promise Bildad had no room for."

"Hungerbitten as a picture of strength gnawed away from within."
